adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The town council met on a cold evening in the middle of the month to talk about the budget for the coming year. Most of the seats in the hall were full, and the people who had come waited quietly while the clerk read the minutes of the last meeting. The first item on the list was the repair of the bridge near the old mill, which had been closed since the spring flood. The engineer explained that the stone work was sound but that the road surface would have to be replaced, and that the work could not begin until the water level fell. Several residents asked about the cost and whether the work would be finished before the school year started. The council said it would seek three offers and report back at the next meeting.

Next came the question of the reading room in the old library. The room had been open on most days of the week for many years, and a small group of people used it to read the papers and to look at the records of the town. The head of the library said that the number of visitors had fallen and that the cost of keeping the room open could no longer be met from the usual funds. She proposed that the room close on two days of the week and that the money saved be used to buy new books for the shelves near the door. Some members of the council said that this would be hard on the people who came to read, and asked whether a group of people from the town could help with the work. The council agreed to look into this and to ask for offers from any group that wished to help.

The last item was the state of the paths in the park by the river. The paths had been muddy since the winter, and many people had written to the council to say that they could no longer walk there with their children or their dogs. The council said that new stone would be laid in the spring and that the work would take about six weeks. A man in the back of the hall asked whether the trees along the path would be kept, and the council said that they would.

When the list was finished, the clerk asked whether anyone else wished to speak. The last person to rise was a retired teacher named Gödel, who asked the council to keep the reading room open on Saturdays and said that he would help pay for the books himself.
